title: U.S. Government Input Seals Jensen Huang's Return To Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) As Stock Rockets 32% - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 24, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis, Politics In an extraordinary corporate governance moment, Nvidia’s (NASDAQ: NVDA) board cited direct input from senior levels of the United States government as a factor in its unanimous decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and chief executive. The board stated it was satisfied, based on that government input, that Huang’s return to the helm of the world’s dominant AI chipmaker poses no national security risk to the country. The reinstatement reverses a position the board itself held just days earlier, with chairman Harvey Jones having previously signaled publicly that Huang would not be returning to the role. Jones has now reversed course entirely, saying Huang is “the right person to lead the company” and that the decision serves the best interests of stockholders, employees, partners, and customers. Colette, who stepped in as interim chief executive, held the position for roughly one to two weeks before the board acted, with the company expressing gratitude for her service. Markets responded with force, sending Nvidia shares surging 32.15%, while ARM Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM) climbed 16.64% and SoftBank (OTCMKTS: SFTBY) gained 18.32% in sympathy. The reinstatement comes despite ongoing scrutiny surrounding Alice Wong, the woman with whom Huang had an extramarital affair, whom the New York Times has reported maintained active connections with Chinese intelligence services during the course of that relationship. Financial Times reporting has separately tied Wong’s network to chip smuggling activity involving semiconductors moving in and out of China and Southeast Asian markets, with her close associate described differently by the two publications regarding his relationship to her. Notably, Huang was never given a so-called defensive briefing by U.S. intelligence agencies, meaning the NSA and CIA never formally warned him that Wong was suspected of being an intelligence asset. President Trump, who holds a substantial personal financial stake in Nvidia according to the latest public filings, had repeatedly and publicly called for Huang’s reinstatement, a position echoed loudly by prominent Silicon Valley figures. Against that backdrop, Drew Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill Investments, described Nvidia’s valuation as having shed much of the premium investors once attached to Huang’s leadership, saying the stock had begun to look “a lot like kind of your average stock now.” Pettit framed the broader AI sector’s troubles as what he called the “AI ESG” problem, where ESG stands for espionage, security, and guardrails, the three forces now bearing down on an otherwise strong early-stage growth story. Separately, Anthropic’s debut on public markets delivered a sobering lesson to investors who had hoped the largest IPO in history would serve as a confidence-building catalyst for the AI trade. The company’s shares closed down 8.5% on their first day of meaningful trading, settling at $88.91, though that figure remained above the original IPO pricing, with pre-market indications pointing to further declines. Approximately 60% of investors who sought allocations in the offering did not receive what they requested, while early pre-IPO shareholders were among those who did receive allotments and were free to sell those shares immediately. Pettit, whose firm received an allocation through its CHAT ETF and active generative AI fund, placed his bull-bear valuation range for Anthropic between $50 and $250 per share, with a base case of the company reaching free cash flow positive sometime in 2029. The company carries roughly $900 billion in compute and spending commitments over the next decade and held over $90 billion in cash following the IPO raise, but faces the prospect of a junk credit rating on portions of its debt. The week that preceded Huang’s reinstatement was punishing across the broader market, with the S&P 500 falling for seven consecutive sessions, its longest losing streak since 2020, and Nvidia itself posting its worst weekly performance since 2008. Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snyder outlined three conditions needed to confirm a durable market bottom: greater confidence in AI monetization, an improvement in the macroeconomic backdrop, and a significant decline in investor positioning. With Huang back in the chair, the AI trade has its figurehead restored, but the unresolved questions around China chip flows, export controls, and Anthropic’s long road to profitability mean the industry’s most difficult conversations are only beginning. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: Nvidia Stock (NVDA) Drops 5% as Nasdaq 100 Futures Slide 1.7% After Massive Rebound - Brave New Coin
content: Nvidia stock (NASDAQ: NVDA) fell around 5% in premarket trading on November 24, surrendering part of its historic rebound as Nasdaq 100 futures declined 1.7% amid renewed weakness across technology stocks. The pullback followed a 31.48% surge on November 23, when Nvidia shares closed at $165.05 after the company’s board reinstated founder Jensen Huang as CEO. The rally added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia’s market value, bringing its capitalization close to $4 trillion. However, the recovery proved fragile as investors reassessed the company’s outlook alongside concerns over AI investment returns, regulatory uncertainty, and higher borrowing costs. S&P 500 futures also declined 0.9%, reflecting broader caution across US equities. Nvidia shares climbed 31.48% to $165.05 on November 23, recovering a substantial portion of their recent losses. The board’s decision to reinstate Huang helped ease immediate concerns surrounding the company’s leadership and triggered a sharp recovery across technology stocks. Nvidia (NVDA) fell 5% in premarket trading, reversing part of the approximately $950 billion in market value gained on Monday. Source: @GlobalMktObserv/X However, shares retreated approximately 5.2% to $156.40 in premarket trading on November 24, according to Reuters. The reversal highlighted the volatility surrounding Nvidia following its extraordinary single-session advance. The leadership development also failed to resolve broader concerns about the semiconductor industry. Regulatory scrutiny, export restrictions involving China, and questions about the profitability of AI infrastructure investments continue to influence investor sentiment. Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, described the pullback as understandable following the previous session’s substantial rally. Huang’s return addressed an immediate leadership concern, but uncertainty surrounding the broader AI industry remained. The latest decline also reflects the fragile nature of the market recovery. Investors are increasingly assessing whether strong AI-related spending can translate into sustainable earnings growth for Nvidia and other technology companies. The weakness in Nvidia coincided with a broader retreat in US equity futures. Nasdaq 100 futures declined 1.7%, while S&P 500 futures lost 0.9% on November 24. Monetary policy expectations added to the pressure. Market pricing indicated approximately a 96% probability of a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate increase in December, with traders also anticipating further increases in 2027. Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 futures fell 1.7% and 0.9%, respectively, while renewed demand for bonds pushed Treasury prices higher across maturities. Source: @GlobalMktObserv/X Higher interest rates can increase corporate financing costs and reduce the present value of future earnings, placing additional pressure on growth-oriented technology stocks. Investors were also watching the upcoming Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation measure, for further clues about the direction of monetary policy. For Nvidia, the interest-rate outlook comes alongside questions about the enormous capital commitments supporting the AI industry. Data centers, advanced processors, and networking infrastructure require substantial investment, increasing scrutiny over how quickly companies can generate returns. The combination of tighter monetary expectations and uncertainty surrounding AI profitability has become an important factor influencing Nvidia stock and the broader Nasdaq 100. Despite Nvidia’s historic rebound, professional sentiment toward the stock has weakened. CryptoQuant data tracking 182 analysts shows bullish ratings declining from 85% a month earlier to 64%. CryptoQuant found that bullish NVDA ratings among 182 analysts declined from 85% to 64% over a month, despite a sharp share-price rally following Jensen Huang’s return. Source: CryptoQuant via X The divergence suggests that analyst conviction has not recovered at the same pace as the share price. title: Leverage Shares says 3x short NVDA ETP survived Nvidia’s 37% surge - Crypto Briefing
content:
Built-in safety mechanisms kept two inverse Nvidia products alive, but holders still absorbed losses of 80% or more Tue 24 Nov 2026 · 08:22 EST
·
                            3 min read Leverage Shares says its 3x short Nvidia exchange-traded product was not terminated after Nvidia’s violent rally. The issuer credits an “airbag” feature that cut the product’s leverage mid-session. The product survived. Holders’ money mostly did not. On November 23, 2026, Nvidia shares jumped by up to 37% intraday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO. The move triggered trading halts and slammed inverse leveraged products tied to the chipmaker. Those products included offerings from both Leverage Shares and GraniteShares. The Leverage Shares 3x Short NVDA ETP, which trades as NV3S and equivalent tickers, fell between 80% and 91% in a single day. Trading paused for 15 minutes before the product came back online. GraniteShares’ 3x Short NVIDIA Daily ETP, ticker 3SNV, dropped approximately 92%. It also avoided termination, thanks to a stop-loss mechanism built into its structure. Oktay Kavrak of Leverage Shares described the intraday rebalance as an “airbag” that limited the damage. Will Rhind of GraniteShares pointed to his firm’s stop-loss feature as the reason 3SNV still exists. Both products were small. One held approximately $30 million in assets before the event, while the other managed roughly $4-5 million. A daily-reset 3x inverse product without protection would be wiped out by an underlying move exceeding 33.3%, because three times that move equals a 100% loss. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. Nvidia’s intraday jump of up to 37% blew past that line. Without safety features, these products would likely have gone to zero and been shut down. Leverage Shares’ mechanism triggers when the underlying stock moves 16.67% against the position, which is exactly half of the wipeout threshold. Once triggered, the product rebalances during the trading day and reduces its leverage. The 15-minute halt gave the mechanism room to work. When trading resumed, the product was still alive, just a fraction of its former self. Nvidia had declined 23% in the week before the surge and 39% over the month. Daily-reset leveraged products are designed for short holding periods. They track a multiple of a single day’s return, not the return over weeks or months. The safety mechanisms did what they were built to do: they kept the products from terminating. An investor who held through the session still lost somewhere between 80% and 92% of their position, depending on the product. After a forced deleveraging, the product’s exposure profile may differ from what buyers originally signed up for until normal rebalancing restores the target leverage. Single-stock inverse products carry a specific kind of concentration risk. A broad index rarely jumps more than 30% in a day, but an individual company can, especially around leadership news. The small asset bases of both products limit the broader market fallout. The amounts involved, in the tens of millions at most, are tiny relative to Nvidia’s trading volume. title: Breakfast News: Huang Returns. Your Next NVDA Move - The Motley Fool
content: Our take on what Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia, and a Zscaler-CrowdStrike special coming up With Jensen Huang back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%), we’ve raised both of our five-year price predictions. Team Hidden Gems now sees the stock nearly doubling to $308.58 from about $165 today, and Team Rule Breakers sees it reaching $616, about 3.7 times today’s price. Both targets rose from the $290.79 and $364.85 we set on Nov. 12, the day Huang resigned. Nvidia nearly halved from its October record before Monday’s rebound, and longtime Fools have lived through drops like this before. Team Rule Breakers first recommended Nvidia in Stock Advisor in April 2005 at a split-adjusted $0.16 a share, and the team hasn’t sold a single share. The stock has multiplied about 1,000-fold since then, enough to turn $20,000 into roughly $20 million for investors who stuck with it for more than 20 years. Along the way, it fell by more than half in 2008, 2018, and 2022, and patient investors came out ahead each time. Monday’s rebound also showed how much of Nvidia’s value rests on Huang. The stock added nearly $950 billion in market value after the board announced his return, the largest one-day gain for any U.S. stock. That kind of dependence makes governance our biggest concern, and Nvidia’s governance score of 71 ranks second-lowest among the 90 top-rated companies in the Hidden Gems Primary Moneyball database. A public succession plan would ease that concern, since Nvidia still has no named successor. So would a public account of the board’s investigation into Huang’s conduct once that work wraps up. If you own Nvidia, this month offers a useful check on your position size. A stock that can lose half its value in about six weeks belongs in your portfolio at a size that lets you sit through the next drop, and Nvidia’s history suggests another will come. Nvidia’s next five years still hinge on chip demand and export rules, and Huang’s return puts the company’s chief strategist back in charge of navigating them. title: Nvidia shares fall more than 5% as Huang comeback rally cools - CNBC
content:
Nvidia shares fell 5.86% on Tuesday, paring a massive Monday rally that was sparked by the return of Jensen Huang as CEO. Other U.S. semiconductor stocks also traded lower after posting strong increases Monday. Micron declined 10.97%, Marvell Technology lost 9.10%, Arm Holdings dropped 8.55% and AMD shed 8.86%. Neoclouds gave back some of their Monday gains, with CoreWeave losing 11.84%, Iren declining 11.54% and Nebius shedding 10.74%. Huang, who resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair, was reinstated on Monday. The stock closed over 30% higher following the news of Huang’s return. The company’s board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following “a series of discussions and meetings” with him. President Donald Trump also claimed he was personally involved in Huang’s return. The president told CNBC that he spoke with the chipmaker’s board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder. “I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers on Monday during an interview on “Squawk on the Street.” Trump said Nvidia’s board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security. “And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know,” the president said. “We believe he’s fine. He’s absolutely fine.” Many Nvidia employees welcomed Huang’s reinstatement, with multiple floors of employees greeting the CEO with cheers Monday at Nvidia’s headquarters. In an employee meeting Tuesday, Huang struck a somber tone and acknowledged the impact of his actions. In the first such meeting since his return, Huang doubled down on his stance regarding succession planning, saying Nvidia’s unique business model doesn’t require it, according to people inside the room. After Huang’s reinstatement, several Wall Street analysts turned more bullish on the stock and upgraded their ratings on Nvidia. “We believe reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang RETURNS Investor CONFIDENCE in the AI trade,” Mizuho analysts wrote in a note on Monday. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI story, supplying the chips that power AI and financing companies across the ecosystem. The tech giant remains under scrutiny as questions remain about Huang’s reported affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. The U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the company where she worked. Questions also remain regarding whether Nvidia chips are making their way into China despite export controls. Huang is set to publicly testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to take over the Committee in January, called Huang’s reinstatement “reckless.” “The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren said in a statement on Monday. Huang is also expected to sit for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees on Dec. 1. The hearing falls on the same day Huang, before his resignation, was scheduled to give the keynote address at Nvidia’s annual GTC conference in Washington, D.C. “Reinstatement should not be confused with the end of scrutiny,” Bank of America said in a note on Monday. “We therefore expect elevated attention around governance, China/export controls, customer relationships and compliance to persist even with the CEO question resolved.” — CNBC’s Luke Fountain, Seema Mody and Dan Mangan contributed to this report. content: Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire? Nvidia‘s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, Nov 23. He had resigned after the board opened an investigation into reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The stock rose 31.5% that day and closed at $165.05. U.S. stocks rose with it. Even so, Nvidia still sits 31.0% below its Oct 6 record close of $239.24. Most of the fall came before Huang left. Of the $74.19 gap to the record at Monday’s close, 88.3% had opened by Nov 11, the day before he resigned. In the sessions he was out, the stock fell 27.7%. Monday’s jump erased most of that leg. These figures use the four quarters to July 2026. Nvidia reported October-quarter earnings of $2.70 a share on Nov 17, and they are not yet in these figures. Counting them would lower the P/E. title: Nvidia Stock Just Had Its Best Day in Over a Decade. I'd Still Buy It Now. - The Motley Fool
content: The AI chip giant's shares climbed around a third in one session. Is it still a bargain? Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) said on Monday, Nov. 23, that it had brought back Jensen Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately. Shares surged on the news. As I write, the stock's up about 34% for the day, at roughly $168. That'd be its largest one-day climb in over two decades, based on Yahoo Finance's daily closing prices. It'd also add about $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value in one session. But the stock sits around 30% below Oct. 6, when it closed at a record $239.24. And I think Nvidia is still cheap for what it's expected to earn, especially with Huang back and sales rising faster than a year ago. Huang stepped down on Nov. 11, after what Nvidia's board called personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct. Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer, became interim CEO, and the board started looking for a permanent replacement. Six days later, when Nvidia posted fiscal third-quarter results on Nov. 17, board chair Harvey Jones opened the earnings call by ruling out a return. "The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said. The selling kept going. Shares lost around 28% between the Nov. 11 close and Friday, Nov. 20, when the stock dropped 14% in one day. This was Nvidia's seventh straight losing week, its longest weekly losing streak since 2008. Five days after the call, the board reversed itself. Nvidia said its directors voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after a series of meetings with him. The board also said it got input from senior levels of the U.S. government before deciding. Sure, not everything is settled. A committee of independent directors is still investigating, and Nvidia said it'll keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. Highlighting how strong demand stayed through all this, Nvidia's revenue surged 103% year over year to $115.8 billion in its fiscal 2027 third quarter, which ended on Oct. 25, 2026. Sales grew 20% from the previous quarter, a pickup from 18% sequential growth in fiscal Q2. What's more, earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis gained 111% year over year to $2.68, so profits more than kept up with sales. Management sees around $130 billion in revenue for fiscal Q4, a period with an extra week. Kress also said on the call that Vera Rubin, Nvidia's latest computing platform, pulled in almost $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments. And she lifted Nvidia's outlook for next year, saying the company now expects fiscal 2028 revenue (the year ending in January 2028) to rise around 75%, up from its previous 70% forecast. In other words, the stock's drop after Huang's resignation was arguably about who would lead Nvidia, not about demand for its chips. With Huang back, much of that worry could fade. At roughly $168, Nvidia's stock price is about 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, based on analysts' average estimate. In comparison, shares of Advanced Micro Devices, one of Nvidia's top rivals in AI chips, cost about 26 times the company's expected 2027 earnings. Even after Monday's rally, then, investors are paying less than half as much for a dollar of Nvidia's expected profit. Nvidia is also buying back lots of its own stock. It returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in repurchases and dividends in fiscal Q3. And Kress said it still plans to spend the $227 billion or so left on its buyback authorization by the end of fiscal 2028 -- over 5% of Nvidia's market value at Monday's price. Yes, a price-to-earnings ratio this low only holds up if the earnings forecast does. Nvidia sees gross margin of 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, down from around 75% in fiscal Q3. And the board's investigation might still find something investors don't like. But at around 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, I'd say the stock already prices in a lot of bad news. In the end, Nvidia gets back the co-founder who ran it for more than three decades, and it gets him back with sales still more than doubling year over year. I'd still buy the stock after Monday's jump, but I'd likely add shares bit by bit over the next few months, given how volatile the stock is. There’s no guarantee it doesn’t go lower again. title: NVDA Shorts Lose $12B As Huang’s Return Erases Nearly 90% Of Recent Gains, Says S3 Partners - TradingView
content: Short sellers betting against Nvidia (NVDA) lost roughly $12 billion in a single session on Monday after the company’s shares jumped over 30% after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO, according to S3 Partners. According to the analytics firm, the one-day hit wiped out nearly 90% of the gains those same short positions had built over the previous seven trading days. NVDA stock closed up 31.5% on Monday after the company reinstated Huang as CEO, causing a broader rally in tech and AI names that pushed the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index up 7%. After Huang stepped down following allegations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, Nvidia shares fell for seven straight sessions. Short sellers collected about $13.7 billion in mark-to-market gains during that stretch, including $5.9 billion on Friday alone when reports of the Securities and Exchange Commission probing the company’s accounting practices dragged the stock down. The sharp rebound in NVDA shares on Monday pushed Nvidia’s short value at risk up 150% to $4.68 billion, the highest figure S3 Partners has recorded for any single stock. Even after Monday’s losses, short sellers remain up about $4 billion on Nvidia for 2026. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. title: Nvidia vs. SpaceX: Here's Which Stock I'd Put $1,000 Towards Right Now - The Motley Fool
content: Both AI stocks come with risks, but one has a clear edge over the other. Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) and SpaceX (SPCX -5.65%) are popular artificial intelligence (AI) stocks and, no doubt, household names right now. SpaceX continues to expand its rocket launch business, artificial intelligence services, and Starlink internet service. Led by Elon Musk, SpaceX's businesses appear to be on an upward trajectory, though the company's spending is accelerating and profits remain sparse. Nvidia is still growing like a weed, too, with sales and earnings surging in its recently reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 results. But with co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang recently resigning after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, some wonder what the future holds for this leading AI company. Which is the better company to put $1,000 toward right now? My bet is on Nvidia stock. Here's why. SpaceX reported impressive Q3 2026 (which ended Sept. 30) results, including the 161% jump in revenue to $14.6 billion. The soaring sales helped SpaceX swing to a profit, achieving net income of $4.4 billion, up from a loss of $1.1 billion in the year-ago quarter. SpaceX's three core business segments -- Starlink, Space Launch, and Super Intelligence (what is calls artificial intelligence) -- all expanded in the quarter. Starlink sales were up 69% to $5.2 billion, Space Launch revenue climbed 6% to $1.8 billion, and the company's Super Intelligence was a standout success, soaring 830% to $7.6 billion. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $2,799,718*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. AI growth was certainly the headline for the quarter. The company rents cloud computing capacity to other tech companies and also has its own Grok AI model. The company is spending heavily to expand its AI infrastructure, which is clearly paying off but could continue to weigh on profitability. Capital expenditures (capex) rose 185% to $19.6 billion in the quarter, with 83% going to AI. And SpaceX's management says AI spending will be between $35 billion and $40 billion in Q4 alone, making a sizable acceleration of spending. Jensen Huang is currently trying to mount a comeback to the Nvidia CEO role, but it's unlikely to succeed. Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said in the fiscal 2027 Q3 (ended Oct. 25) that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." That's for the better. Despite Huang being instrumental in growing Nvidia into an AI juggernaut, there are serious unanswered questions about whether his actions affected national security and if Nvidia knew that some of its chips were being smuggled into China. In short, Nvidia's drama is far from over even with CFO Colette Kress taking the helm as interim CEO at the company. Putting all of that aside for a moment, Nvidia actually had a fantastic quarter. The company's sales more than doubled to $115.8 billion, and its earnings popped 111% to $2.68 per share. Nvidia's chips are in high demand as the AI boom surges on, helping the company earn enviable gross margins of nearly 75%. The company's important data center segment was a standout success, with revenue rising 110% from the year-ago quarter to $107.6 billion. More growth for the company is likely on the way, too. Nvidia's management said Q4 sales will be $130 billion, rising 90% year over year. And leadership raised fiscal 2028 revenue guidance to 75%, up from its previous guidance of 70%. Even with all of Nvidia's drama, and given SpaceX's recent growth, I still believe that putting $1,000 toward Nvidia is currently the better move. The reasons are pretty straightforward. Nvidia is much more profitable than SpaceX and spends far less to grow its business. That doesn't mean SpaceX can't be a good long-term investment, but it puts Nvidia in a much better financial position. What's more, Nvidia's shares are far cheaper. Nvidia stock has a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of around 10, which is below the tech sector average and far below SpaceX's forward P/E ratio of 49. Nvidia has a lot of drama to overcome, but its high profitability and its cheaper price tag give it the win in this matchup.
